Senses.Explanation: To answer when called or to acknowledge an instruction. The word occurs 1,087 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Compilers repeatedly preserve the same audible action as the hinge of an encounter: Nanyang Huizhong calls his attendant three times and receives three answers; Shakyamuni calls Ananda after Ananda asks about the former buddhas' procedure; Mahakasyapa calls Ananda in the robe-transmission case; and Huangbo Xiyun names Pei Xiu by calling him, then declares the naming complete when Pei answers. In Xingsen's record an unnamed lecture master answers the call 'Lecturer,' and Xingsen immediately appraises him. Dahui Zonggao later raises an exchange in which Luoshan calls Zhaoqing and Zhaoqing answers before Luoshan replies 'a macaque enters the site of the Way' (山召大師。慶應諾。山云。獼猴入道場). The same response also acknowledges an instruction: Ananda answers Shakyamuni's order to enter the city with the bowl. The Zen bend is not a special second meaning but the records' placement of this ordinary answer as the next public turn and, at times, the central action of a named case.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend lies in the records' repeated use of the simplest audible answer as the decisive next turn of a public interview or named case. The entry reports that structural deployment without asserting what the answer proves. Answering a call and assenting to an order remain the same response event, not different things.
